newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel calls Clinton remarks on peace encouraging.
newsitem.headline: Israel calls Clinton remarks on peace encouraging.

text.p: Israel said it was "encouraged" by U.S. President Bill Clinton's linkage of its security demands on the Palestinian Authority with a continued peace process following a twin suicide bombing.

Clinton said in Washington on Wednesday that Middle East peacemaking could not proceed unless Israel was convinced Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was doing his utmost to maintain security in the region.

"...Until the Israelis believe that the Palestinian Authority is making 100 percent effort, which is different from 100 percent results, but is making 100 percent effort on security, it is impossible for peace to proceed," Clinton said at a news conference.

Jordan's Crown Prince Hassan proved unable in talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Wednesday to persuade Israel to ease sanctions imposed after the bombings in Jerusalem last week.
They killed 15 people, including the two bombers, in the deadliest attack against Israelis in a year.

In the aftermath, Israel suspended a resumption of its talks with the Palestinians and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, preventing Palestinians from going to their places of work in Israel proper.
Arafat blasted the closure as collective punishment.
"If they begin to fight terrorism, we will review the various steps that were taken in order to make them fight terrorism," Netanyahu said after his talks with Prince Hassan.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said she planned to visit the region at the end of August "provided there is some progress on security issues".
Netanyahu's office said the prime minister and Albright spoke by phone on Wednesday evening.
Netanyahu's communications chief, David Bar-Illan, welcomed the statements made separately out of Washington by Clinton and Albright.

"We are encouraged by the president and secretary's remarks, which make it clear that the Palestinian Authority must join the nations that fight terrorism before the peace process can proceed," Bar-Illan told Reuters.
"We should like to hope that Secretary Albright will have good reason to come in light of what she said that she would make the trip if there is progess on security issues," he said.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross is scheduled to arrive on Saturday for talks focusing on security matters, Israeli government officials said.
Ross was supposed to arrive last week but delayed his trip after the bombings.
Netanyahu, for his part, is expected to visit Jordan next week for talks with King Hussein.
After three hours of talks with Netanyahu, Prince Hassan described the current situation as "a very dangerous crisis".
"There can be no peace without security and there can be no security without peace," he told reporters in Jerusalem.
Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat accused Israel of treating the Palestinians like hostages.

"The Israeli measures indicated the Israeli government's readiness to launch a war on the Palestinian Authority, President Arafat and the Palestinian people, Erekat told a news conference in the West Bank.
Israel announced on Wednesday a slight relaxation of an "internal closure" in the West Bank and Gaza Strip but said the ban on entering the Jewish state remained in force.

The Israeli Army said in a statement Palestinians were allowed to reach workplaces at Jewish settlements and industrial zones in the two areas. It was unclear how many workers were affected by the move.
